# Domain Pitfalls

**Domain:** Programmatic Video Generation + AI Content System for Learning Platform
**Researched:** 2026-05-13

---

## Critical Pitfalls

Mistakes that cause rewrites, blown timelines, or stakeholder demo failures.

---

### Pitfall 1: Choppy "Slideshow" Animations Instead of Fluid Motion

**What goes wrong:** The prototype looks like an animated PowerPoint -- elements snap between states, transitions feel mechanical, and the result screams "generated by code" rather than "produced by a design studio." This is the single biggest risk for stakeholder demos. The animation research contract specifically calls for "fluid physics and natural easing" with "nothing snapping abruptly into place."

**Why it happens:**
- Using `linear` interpolation instead of spring physics or custom easing curves
- Animating layout properties (`width`, `height`, `left`, `top`) instead of GPU-accelerated `transform` and `opacity`
- Not choreographing sequential staging (container slides in, then action triggers, then results fade in) -- everything happens simultaneously or with uniform timing
- Hardcoding frame-based timing instead of using Remotion's `spring()` with proper `fps` from `useVideoConfig()`
- Insufficient animation duration -- professional motion needs 400-800ms per transition, not 200ms

**Consequences:** Stakeholders see a tech demo, not a product. The "wow factor" evaporates. The Anthropic Cowork video reference sets a bar that slide transitions cannot meet.

**Prevention:**
- Use Remotion `spring()` as the primary animation primitive with `damping: 12-15`, `mass: 0.8-1.2` for organic feel
- Animate ONLY `transform` (translate, scale, rotate) and `opacity` -- never layout properties
- Build a reusable `<StaggeredSequence>` component that enforces sequential staging with configurable overlap
- Use Remotion's Timing Editor to visually design curves before coding
- Reference the animation contract: every motion must "educate, guide, or provide feedback" -- remove decorative-only animations
- Build one 10-second hero scene first, get visual approval, then scale the pattern

**Detection:** If you can describe any transition as "X appears" rather than "X glides/floats/settles into place," it is too abrupt. Record the preview at 0.5x speed -- jank becomes obvious.

**Phase relevance:** Phase 1 (prototype). Must be solved in the first scene before scaling to full module.

**Confidence:** HIGH -- based on Remotion documentation, animation contract analysis, and CSS performance best practices.

### Pitfall 2: Docker Rendering Produces Different Output Than Local Development

**What goes wrong:** Animations render smoothly in the Remotion Studio (browser preview) but produce choppy, corrupted, or visually different output when rendered in Docker. Fonts are wrong, colors shift, GPU-accelerated effects break, or the render crashes entirely.

**Why it happens:**
- Headless Chromium disables GPU by default, causing CSS effects like `box-shadow`, `text-shadow`, gradients, `filter: blur()`, and `filter: drop-shadow()` to render orders of magnitude slower or differently
- Docker's default `/dev/shm` is only 64MB; Chrome needs 1-2GB for rendering, causing "Failed to allocate shared memory" crashes
- Docker reports more CPUs than are actually available (e.g., reports 16 but only 4 allocated), causing Remotion to spawn too many Chrome instances and thrash
- Custom fonts (Syne) not installed in the container image -- renders fall back to system sans-serif
- Alpine Linux base images cause 35% slower renders due to Rust component incompatibility
- Windows Docker Desktop volume mounts from NTFS are 10-20x slower than native Linux filesystem

**Consequences:** "Works on my machine" syndrome. The prototype looks great in preview, but the final MP4 is broken. Days lost debugging container issues instead of building content.

**Prevention:**
- Set `--shm-size=2g` on every `docker run` command
- Explicitly set `--cpus` and `--cpuset-cpus` to match actual allocation
- Use `node:22-bookworm-slim` base image (never Alpine)
- Install Syne font in Dockerfile: copy font files to `/usr/local/share/fonts/` and run `fc-cache -f -v`
- Also install Chrome dependencies: `libnss3 libdbus-1-3 libatk1.0-0 libgbm-dev libasound2`
- Replace GPU-heavy CSS effects with precomputed PNG/SVG images for Docker renders
- Store project files in WSL2 filesystem (`/home/user/`), NOT Windows filesystem (`/mnt/c/`), for 20x better I/O
- Always test with a 5-10 second clip first before rendering the full module

**Detection:** Run `npx remotion benchmark` inside Docker and compare to local. If Docker is >3x slower, configuration is wrong. Check `chrome://gpu` status in the container.

**Phase relevance:** Phase 1 (environment setup). Must be solved before any rendering work begins.

**Confidence:** HIGH -- based on official Remotion Docker documentation, CrePal Docker guide, and Windows Docker performance issue reports.

### Pitfall 3: Video File Exceeds Teachable's 2GB Limit

**What goes wrong:** A polished, high-quality 10-15 minute Module 1 video renders at >2GB and cannot be uploaded to Teachable. Or the video is under 2GB but Teachable re-encodes it, destroying quality.

**Why it happens:**
- Remotion's default H.264 CRF is 18 (high quality, large files). A 10-minute 1080p/30fps video at CRF 18 can easily reach 1.5-3GB depending on scene complexity
- Animations with many moving elements, gradients, and color transitions produce high-bitrate frames
- Not accounting for the difference between animation-heavy content (high bitrate) vs. talking-head video (low bitrate)
- Using PNG frame format instead of JPEG during render (larger intermediary files, slower encode)

**Consequences:** Last-minute scramble to re-encode or split the video. Quality compromises. Upload failures on demo day.

**Prevention:**
- Target CRF 23 for H.264 (good quality, ~40% smaller than CRF 18). Test with CRF 20, 23, 25 on a sample scene to find the sweet spot
- Use `--video-bitrate 5M` as a hard cap (5 Mbps = ~375MB per 10 minutes)
- If the module is long, split into sub-lessons (5-7 min each) rather than one monolithic video. This also improves learner engagement
- Use `--x264-preset slow` for better compression at the same quality (trades render time for file size)
- Render at exactly 1920x1080 and 30fps -- do not over-spec
- Build a post-render validation step: check file size, resolution, codec, and duration before considering the render "done"
- Teachable's highest playback resolution is 720p, so if file size is still too large, rendering at 720p is acceptable with no visible quality loss on the platform

**Detection:** Add a CI/build step that fails if output exceeds 1.8GB (leave 200MB safety margin).

**Phase relevance:** Phase 1 (rendering pipeline). Encoding settings must be established in the pipeline configuration from day one.

**Confidence:** HIGH -- Teachable's 2GB limit confirmed via official help docs; Remotion encoding settings documented.

### Pitfall 4: Syne Font Renders Incorrectly or Falls Back to System Font

**What goes wrong:** The brand's Syne font renders as Arial/Helvetica in the video, or only some weights load (400 but not 700/800), or the font loads in preview but not in the Docker render. The result looks generic and off-brand.

**Why it happens:**
- `loadFont()` from `@remotion/google-fonts/Syne` loads ALL weights and subsets by default, which can cause timeout errors
- Font files referenced with raw paths instead of `staticFile()` fail to resolve during render
- `loadFont()` called inside a component render function instead of at module top level
- Docker container missing font installation -- fontconfig cache not rebuilt
- Google Fonts CDN blocked or slow in the Docker network environment

**Consequences:** Every frame looks wrong. Brand consistency -- a stated non-negotiable constraint -- is violated. Fixing requires re-rendering the entire video.

**Prevention:**
- Use `@remotion/google-fonts/Syne` with explicit weight filtering: `loadFont({ weights: ['400', '600', '700', '800'] })` at module top level
- For Docker reliability, ALSO install Syne as a local font: download the `.ttf` files, copy to `public/fonts/`, and load via `@remotion/fonts` with `staticFile('fonts/Syne-Regular.ttf')`
- Create a `<BrandText>` wrapper component that enforces `fontFamily` from the loaded font's return value
- Add a visual regression test: render a single "font check" frame and compare against a reference screenshot
- In Dockerfile, install fonts and rebuild cache as a separate layer for caching

**Detection:** Render a single frame with all font weights displayed. Compare against brand reference. Automate this as the first render step.

**Phase relevance:** Phase 1 (environment setup + component library). Font loading must be validated before building any scenes.

**Confidence:** HIGH -- Remotion font documentation, `@remotion/google-fonts` API, and Docker font installation guides all confirm these patterns.

### Pitfall 5: Timeline Pressure Causes "Demo Mode" Architecture That Cannot Scale

**What goes wrong:** Under stakeholder demo deadline pressure, the team hardcodes scene content, skips the storyboard metadata system, builds monolithic animation files, and produces a polished video that cannot be regenerated when content changes. The "pipeline" is actually a one-shot script.

**Why it happens:**
- Stakeholder meetings in days, not weeks
- Natural instinct to "just make it work" for the demo
- Storyboard metadata and content-to-animation pipeline feel like overhead when you need one video
- Confusing "prototype" with "throwaway" -- the prototype IS the foundation

**Consequences:** After the stakeholder demo, the team has a pretty video but no system. Rebuilding Module 1 for voiceover integration requires starting over. Scaling to later modules requires rewriting everything. The "content that stays current" promise in the roadmap is a lie.

**Prevention:**
- Enforce a minimal scene abstraction from day one: each scene is a React component that receives `props` (content text, timing data, asset paths) -- never hardcode text strings in animation code
- Create a `timeline.json` structure even for the prototype -- scene ID, start frame, duration, content reference, voiceover placeholder slot
- Separate concerns into three layers from the start:
  1. Content layer (markdown/JSON with the actual educational text)
  2. Storyboard layer (timing, scene sequence, transition types)
  3. Animation layer (React components that render from storyboard data)
- The prototype can have only 5-6 scenes; the architecture does not need to be complete. But the data flow pattern must exist.
- Budget: spend 20% of prototype time on structure, 80% on visual polish. This is NOT 50/50 -- the demo must look good.

**Detection:** Ask: "Can I change the text in Scene 3 without editing the animation component?" If no, the architecture is wrong.

**Phase relevance:** Phase 1 (architecture). The very first scene must establish the pattern; subsequent scenes follow it.

**Confidence:** HIGH -- universal pattern in startup prototyping, reinforced by project requirements for content-to-animation pipeline and voiceover-ready metadata.

## Moderate Pitfalls

---

### Pitfall 6: Windows + Docker Desktop + WSL2 Development Environment Pain

**What goes wrong:** File system operations are 10-20x slower when Docker containers access Windows-mounted volumes. Hot reload is sluggish or broken. Remotion preview updates take seconds instead of milliseconds. Docker Desktop itself consumes excessive RAM.

**Prevention:**
- Clone the repo into the WSL2 filesystem: `\\wsl$\Ubuntu\home\user\project` -- NOT `C:\Users\...\project`
- Configure Docker Desktop to use WSL2 backend (not Hyper-V)
- Allocate at least 8GB RAM and 4 CPUs to WSL2 via `.wslconfig`
- Use VS Code with Remote-WSL extension to edit files natively in Linux filesystem
- Named Docker volumes for `node_modules` to avoid cross-filesystem I/O

**Detection:** If `npm install` takes >60 seconds or Remotion preview refresh takes >3 seconds, you are hitting the filesystem translation penalty.

**Phase relevance:** Phase 1 (environment setup). First task before any code.

**Confidence:** HIGH -- extensively documented Docker for Windows issue (docker/for-win#10476, multiple WSL2 performance guides).

---

### Pitfall 7: Render Time Spiral -- 10-Minute Video Takes Hours to Render

**What goes wrong:** A 10-minute module with complex animations takes 30-60+ minutes to render, making iteration impossible. Each content tweak requires another hour of waiting.

**Why it happens:**
- GPU-accelerated CSS effects (shadows, blurs, gradients) without actual GPU access in Docker
- Concurrency set too high (spawns too many Chrome instances) or too low (underutilizes CPU)
- Using WebM/VP9 codec instead of H.264 (5-10× slower encoding)
- PNG frame format instead of JPEG (larger, slower)
- Heavy JavaScript computation in render path (no memoization)

**Prevention:**
- Replace CSS shadows/blurs with precomputed SVG or PNG assets for Docker renders
- Run `npx remotion benchmark` to find optimal concurrency for your hardware
- Use H.264 codec (default) -- never WebM for production renders
- Use JPEG image format for intermediate frames unless transparency is needed
- Wrap expensive computations in `useMemo()` / `useCallback()`
- Enable `enableMultiProcessOnLinux: true` in Docker
- Consider a two-tier workflow: fast preview renders (720p, CRF 28) for iteration, full-quality renders (1080p, CRF 23) for final output

**Detection:** If a 30-second test clip takes >2 minutes to render in Docker, extrapolate and fix before attempting the full module.

**Phase relevance:** Phase 1 (pipeline optimization). Establish render time benchmarks early.

**Confidence:** HIGH -- Remotion performance docs, CrePal Docker guide, and GitHub issues confirm these patterns.

---

### Pitfall 8: Voiceover Retrofit Breaks Animation Timing

**What goes wrong:** The visual-only prototype has beautiful animation timing. When AI voiceover is added later, the voiceover duration does not match scene duration. Scenes are too short for the narration, or too long with dead air. Retrofitting requires re-timing every scene.

**Why it happens:**
- Animations timed to "look good" rather than to a narration script
- No storyboard metadata capturing scene duration and content density
- TTS output length is unpredictable -- the same text can vary by 20-30% depending on voice, speed, and pauses
- No placeholder audio track used during prototype development
- Viewers notice audio-visual mismatches within 45 milliseconds

**Prevention:**
- Write the narration script for each scene BEFORE timing the animations, even if voiceover is not recorded yet
- Time each scene to the estimated narration duration (rough rule: ~150 words per minute for educational content, so 30 words = ~12 seconds)
- Include a `voiceover` slot in the storyboard metadata: `{ sceneId, narrationText, estimatedDurationSec, audioFile: null }`
- Design animations with flexible "hold" states -- the final state of each animation should be visually stable for variable duration
- When voiceover is added later, use Remotion's `getAudioDuration()` to dynamically size scene duration to match the audio
- Build scene transitions as separate "bridge" sequences that can absorb timing variance

**Detection:** For each scene, ask: "What happens if this needs to be 3 seconds longer?" If the answer is "nothing, it just holds," good. If the answer is "the next animation overlaps," bad.

**Phase relevance:** Phase 1 (metadata design) for the schema. Phase 2+ (voiceover integration) for implementation.

**Confidence:** MEDIUM -- based on TTS timing research and Remotion audio documentation. Exact timing variance depends on TTS provider choice.

### Pitfall 9: Content Currency System Becomes a Full CMS Nobody Asked For

**What goes wrong:** The "content repository that stays current" requirement balloons into building a custom content management system with versioning, diffing, approval workflows, and scheduled updates -- when all that is really needed is a structured folder of markdown files with a cron job that checks vendor docs.

**Why it happens:**
- AI tools change weekly, creating anxiety about content freshness
- Over-engineering the update mechanism before understanding the actual update frequency
- Conflating "detects changes" with "automatically rewrites content"
- Building infrastructure for 100 AI tools when the course covers ~12

**Prevention:**
- Start with the simplest possible structure: one markdown file per AI tool, organized by capability
- Content updates are manual-review-required (per project requirements: "humans approve the diff")
- Automated part is DETECTION only: weekly script compares current vendor docs against stored content, flags diffs
- No auto-rewriting of content -- Instructor's teaching philosophy must be preserved
- The accuracy-sweep skill already exists for fact-checking; use it, do not rebuild it

**Detection:** If the content system has more than 3 database tables or requires a web UI to operate, it has been over-scoped.

**Phase relevance:** Phase 2+ (content repository). NOT Phase 1 -- the prototype uses static content.

**Confidence:** MEDIUM -- pattern-based from startup over-engineering, validated by project scope (three separate MVPs defined).

---

### Pitfall 10: Large Conversation Video Transcription Bottleneck

**What goes wrong:** Large source recordings contain critical deliverable details but cannot be transcribed quickly. Whisper API has a 25MB file limit. Extracting audio, chunking, transcribing, and merging takes hours of manual pipeline work, and chunk boundaries corrupt sentences.

**Why it happens:**
- Whisper API hard limit: 25MB per file
- A 2.4GB video's audio track (even as 128kbps MP3) is ~50-100MB, requiring 2-4 chunks minimum
- Chunk boundaries can split mid-sentence, producing garbled transcription at seams
- No existing pipeline for this -- it is a one-time task that feels like it should not need automation

**Prevention:**
- Extract audio with ffmpeg first: `ffmpeg -i video.mp4 -vn -acodec libmp3lame -b:a 128k audio.mp3`
- Split at silence points using ffmpeg's `silencedetect` filter, NOT at fixed durations
- For 2.4GB video: expect 60-90 minutes of audio, split into 8-12 chunks of 5-10 minutes each
- Use local Whisper (not API) if a capable GPU is available -- no file size limit
- Alternatively, use a service like AssemblyAI or Deepgram that accepts large files directly via URL
- Process chunks in parallel, then merge with overlap handling (50ms crossfade at boundaries)
- This is a one-time task -- do not build an automated transcription pipeline

**Detection:** If transcription is blocking prototype development, the priority is wrong. Transcribe asynchronously while building animations with available content.

**Phase relevance:** Pre-Phase 1 (context gathering). Should be done in parallel with environment setup.

**Confidence:** HIGH -- Whisper API 25MB limit is documented by OpenAI; ffmpeg chunking is standard practice.

## Minor Pitfalls

---

### Pitfall 11: Brand Color Drift in Video Encoding

**What goes wrong:** The warm Soft Linen (#EDE8E3) background appears slightly yellow or grey in the rendered MP4 due to color space conversion during H.264 encoding. Crimson (#8B2635) accent appears darker or more saturated than intended.

**Prevention:**
- H.264 uses YUV color space, which can shift RGB values. Use `-pix_fmt yuv420p` (standard) and add `-colorspace bt709 -color_trc bt709 -color_primaries bt709` to ffmpeg flags
- Remotion allows passing custom ffmpeg flags via `--ffmpeg-override`
- Render a color test frame (brand palette swatches) and compare against hex values in an image editor
- Accept that minor shifts are inevitable -- the difference is usually <2% and imperceptible on typical displays

**Phase relevance:** Phase 1 (pipeline). One-time calibration during encoding setup.

**Confidence:** MEDIUM -- color space conversion is a known video encoding concern; exact impact depends on display and player.

---

### Pitfall 12: Remotion Version Lock and Breaking Changes

**What goes wrong:** Starting with Remotion v3 patterns when v4 is current, or upgrading mid-project and hitting breaking API changes (e.g., `<Html5Video>` deprecated in favor of `<Video>`, `@remotion/fonts` only available from v4.0.164+).

**Prevention:**
- Pin to the latest stable Remotion v4 from day one
- Use `<Video>` component (not deprecated `<Html5Video>` or `<OffthreadVideo>`)
- Use `@remotion/google-fonts` for Syne (type-safe, optimized)
- Lock versions in `package.json` -- no `^` ranges for Remotion packages
- Check Remotion changelog before starting: https://www.remotion.dev/changelog

**Phase relevance:** Phase 1 (environment setup). Pin versions at project initialization.

**Confidence:** HIGH -- based on Remotion documentation noting deprecated APIs and version-specific features.

---

### Pitfall 13: Overusing Motion -- Animation Fatigue

**What goes wrong:** Every element bounces, slides, and fades. The video feels hyperactive and distracting rather than calm and professional. The "warm minimalist" aesthetic is drowned in motion noise.

**Prevention:**
- Apply the animation contract rule: "If an animation does not improve the user experience or clarify how a feature works, it should be removed"
- Limit to 2-3 active animations per scene maximum
- Background elements should be static or near-static; only the focal element moves
- Use longer, slower animations (600-1000ms) rather than many fast ones
- Test by watching with a non-technical person: if they say "that was busy," reduce motion

**Phase relevance:** Phase 1 (scene design). Applies to every scene.

**Confidence:** HIGH -- based on animation research document's "purpose-driven motion" principle and Apple/Google animation guidelines.

## Phase-Specific Warnings

| Phase Topic | Likely Pitfall | Mitigation |
|-------------|---------------|------------|
| Environment Setup | Windows Docker filesystem penalty (#6) | Store project in WSL2 filesystem from minute one |
| Environment Setup | Docker Chrome missing dependencies (#2) | Use Remotion's recommended Dockerfile with all deps |
| Environment Setup | Font loading failures (#4) | Validate font rendering with single-frame test before building scenes |
| Prototype Scenes | Choppy animations (#1) | Build one hero scene, get approval, then replicate pattern |
| Prototype Scenes | Animation fatigue (#13) | Apply "purpose-driven motion" filter to every animation |
| Prototype Scenes | Hardcoded content (#5) | Props-driven components from scene one, even for prototype |
| Rendering Pipeline | Docker output differs from preview (#2) | Run benchmark in Docker early; compare against local |
| Rendering Pipeline | File exceeds 2GB (#3) | Set `--video-bitrate 5M` and validate size in CI |
| Rendering Pipeline | Color drift (#11) | Render brand palette test frame during pipeline setup |
| Rendering Pipeline | Slow render times (#7) | Benchmark concurrency, use two-tier quality workflow |
| Voiceover Integration | Timing mismatch (#8) | Narration script + flexible hold states from prototype |
| Content Repository | Over-engineering into CMS (#9) | Start with markdown files + detection-only automation |
| Pre-Production | Transcription bottleneck (#10) | Extract audio, chunk at silence, process in parallel |
